description: We’re a team of Applied Mathematics undergraduates at IE University. Between us we cover mathematical modelling, statistics and data analysis, and coding in Python, and vibecoding. We’re also confident public speakers, so we enjoy turning technical work into a clear, convincing pitch. Our team is already complete and we’re not looking for new members right now, but we’re happy to connect and swap ideas with other participants during the hackathon!
summary:
Moon bases are planned at 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi, where materials ignite more easily. Yet no solid material in NASA's public data has been burned in microgravity above 22% oxygen. Ember in Freefall makes gaps like this visible.

We turned 1,624 runs from 24 investigations in NASA's 7.8 TB combustion archive into one checked dataset, and cut real flame footage out of the raw experiment videos. Pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base or rover) or set oxygen, pressure, airflow and gravity: the site ranks relevant investigations and plays a live flame simulation next to real NASA footage of the closest experiment. The simulation is tuned on NASA outcomes and flame shapes from 384 NASA videos, and a neural network trained on it answers instantly. On NASA experiments it was not trained on, it correctly predicted whether a fire keeps burning or goes out 30 times out of 31. In 3D ISS and Moon base interiors, you can set objects on fire with fans on or off. Ember, our AI assistant, answers questions citing NASA sources.

Crews heading to the Moon need to know which fire risks are backed by data and which are guesses. We show both.
details:
Check out our GitHub repository too: https://github.com/Alexzcoder/flame-in-freefall

WHAT IT DOES

Ember in Freefall answers one question for anyone designing a crewed habitat: if a small fire starts in this cabin atmosphere, what has NASA actually tested, what will the fire do, and how much should we trust that answer?

You pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurized rover, spacesuit, Apollo 1...) or set oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity and fuel type yourself. The site then:

1. Shows where your conditions sit on a "gap map" of every NASA microgravity combustion run, and how many real experiments are close by.

2. Ranks the 24 NASA combustion investigations by how relevant they are to your habitat, and explains why each one ranks where it does.

3. Plays a live fluid simulation of a flame next to real NASA footage of the closest experiment.

4. Lets you walk through 3D ISS and Moon base interiors and set objects on fire (crew quarters, cable bundles, cargo bags) to see whether the fire survives with the fans on or off, how fast it spreads, and how far other flammables should be kept away.

5. Answers questions through Ember, an AI assistant that cites the NASA run, report page or paper behind every claim.

Our headline finding: no solid material in NASA's public data has been burned in microgravity above 22.2% oxygen, yet Moon bases are planned at 30%+ oxygen and 10.2 psi. Our tool makes that gap impossible to miss.

HOW IT WORKS

Data pipeline (Python, pandas). We pulled the run tables of 9 NASA PSI investigations (FLEX, CFI, CFI-G, Flame Design, SPICE, BASS-II, SAFFIRE I-III) into one typed schema: 1,624 runs, 633 with measured outcomes, plus metadata for all 24 combustion investigations. Every value links back to its source file and row, and 5,123 numbers were re-read from the raw NASA files to check them. We handled the traps a naive merge would miss: unknown is never treated as zero, censored burn times (crew stopped a still-burning flame) are flagged, inverse flames (oxygen flowing out of the burner) are separated, and cabin pressure or oxygen that NASA didn't record is marked as assumed on every run.

Real footage from NASA's 7.8 TB archive. PSI video links are signed S3 URLs, so we stream only what we need. For each video we find the burn automatically from frame brightness: the lab lights switch off right before ignition, then the flame shows up as bright pixels against the dark background. We picked 25 runs spread across the condition space (farthest-point sampling), cut a clip around ignition, brightened the very dim blue flames, cropped to the flame and denoised. 23 clips are on the site; 2 gas runs were dropped because the flame was buried in sensor noise. For the models we streamed about 90 GB of video and kept the burn frames of 457 runs (BASS-II, CFI, CFI-G), measuring each flame's shape with OpenCV: stretch, fill, ring shape, blue share and flicker. All shape measures are ratios, because NASA cameras have no scale in the frame.

Flame simulation. A 2D stable-fluids solver (semi-Lagrangian advection, Jacobi pressure projection, vorticity confinement) with one-step combustion (fuel + oxygen -> heat + soot, only where hot). Buoyancy scales with gravity, so the flame shape comes from the physics: tall and flickering at 1 g, a dim sphere fed only by diffusion at 0 g that can starve itself of oxygen when the fan is off, as NASA's BASS-II saw. It runs in the browser in WebGL2 shaders, and as a batched PyTorch port on the GPU that simulates hundreds of NASA runs in one call.

Calibration against NASA. We fit 14 physics knobs with the cross-entropy method (16 candidates per generation, all candidates x all runs in one GPU batch) against 331 CFI-G gas-flame outcomes, BASS-II flame shapes from video, and 31 solid burn-or-go-out cases. Whole test days are held out. In leave-one-out testing, the calibrated model predicts whether a solid fire keeps burning or goes out in 30 of 31 cases it never saw (the hand-tuned starting version got 18 of 31). A fuel-spread mode (fuel that heats, releases vapour and burns out) is fitted to 7 spread targets from the BASS-II summary report and SAFFIRE-II, matching 6 of 7 (fabric 2.38 mm/s vs NASA's 2.1-2.6).

Neural-network emulator. We ran the calibrated simulation 20,000 times across habitat-relevant conditions and trained an ensemble of 3 small neural networks (PyTorch, 3 x 192 SiLU layers, flame image compressed to 48 principal components). The weights are exported to JSON and run in plain JavaScript, so the site predicts a flame instantly. On 2,000 held-out simulations it predicts ignition in 99.4% and extinction in 97.9% of cases. Disagreement between the 3 networks flags where it is unsure.

Data-only models. Gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn) predict gas-flame and droplet outcomes directly from NASA tables, with 5-fold cross-validation grouped by test day and calibrated 80% ranges. Gas-flame extinction time is typically off by x1.42 (guessing: x2.67); droplet burning rate has a median error of 0.040 mm2/s (guessing: 0.095). Each prediction says whether it is inside the conditions NASA tested.

Habitat risk. For fire spreading between objects we use standard fire-engineering radiation estimates (point-source heat flux vs. each material's critical heat flux) with Monte Carlo over uncertain material values, which gives a safe separation distance per object.

Ranking. Each investigation gets a 0-100 score: 50% closeness of its runs to your conditions, 20% measured outcomes, 20% cabin relevance (real cabin materials vs. lab fuels), 10% fire-safety focus (prevention, detection, suppression), with reasons and caveats shown.

Ember (AI). A DeepSeek tool-calling agent that never sees the dataset directly: it has to call 6 tools (search documents, find runs, nearest runs, rank, get investigation, compare) and cite what they return. Search covers 1,882 texts (investigation objectives, 299 papers, 1,559 NASA final-report pages) in a SQLite full-text index.

Stack. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch, OpenCV, ffmpeg), FastAPI on Vercel, vanilla JavaScript, WebGL2, Three.js (3D orbit view, habitats, 14 3D models), Plotly, Remotion for the demo video. GPU calibration ran overnight on an RTX-class card.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

NASA's combustion results are spread over 24 investigations and terabytes of tables, video and reports. Our tool turns them into an answer in seconds, with the evidence attached. Habitat designers see exactly where data runs out (high oxygen, low pressure, partial gravity) and can target the next experiments there. Students and researchers get one clean, documented dataset and a search engine with citations. The same physics applies on Earth: aircraft cabins, hyperbaric chambers, oxygen therapy and submarines.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

We didn't just chart the data: we used NASA's own experiment videos twice, once to show people real flames and once as ground truth to tune a physics simulation. Then we compressed that simulation into a neural network small enough to run in a web page. Seeing a simulated flame next to the real NASA flame at the same conditions makes microgravity fire intuitive in a way a table can't. And Ember, a small round blue flame (that's how flames look in microgravity), guides users through the site.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Trust above everything. Every number is labelled as cross-validated, held out or fitted, and our "How we checked" page also lists what did not work: simulated gas-flame outcomes are no better than guessing on unseen test days, so gas and droplet numbers on the site come from the data models instead, and the simulated flame shapes are marked as illustrative. All NASA data is from microgravity, so anything at Moon or Mars gravity is labelled as physics-based extrapolation. Above 22% oxygen there is no solid-material data, and the site says so wherever it matters.
